author: Shaquira Speaks
title: Mental health expert breaks down DeCarlos Brown request for delay in death penalty hearing - NewsBreak
text:
By Shaquira Speaks ,
2 hours ago
CHARLOTTE ( QUEEN CITY NEWS ) — A hearing for DeCarlos Brown and the decision on whether he could face the death penalty may not be held at the end of April.
Brown underwent a mental evaluation in December. The evaluation found he was: “incapable to proceed.”
“When someone is deemed incompetent, it doesn’t mean that they’re not responsible forever. I think that’s important to know. It means that right now they don’t have the mental capacity to understand the charges and to participate in their own defense,” said mental health expert Dr. Charryse Johnson .
Brown’s attorney says his client is also facing federal charges for Iryna Zarutska’s killing last August. The lawyer argues moving forward with a state trial would create a “logistical barrier” because Brown is still in federal custody.
“The judge has to make that determination. And you’re not going to get a competency hearing until you get a Rule 24 hearing. So they’ll have the ‘Rule 24 hearing,’ and it’s not even scheduled yet to have a competency hearing. So you’ll have to have a number of things take place before we can even get to either him being to be deemed competent to go forward or not,” said North Carolina criminal defense attorney and Queen City News Chief Legal Analyst Khalif Rhodes.
Dr. Johnson says the process to declare a patient incapable or incompetent to stand trial is extensive.
Photo: Decarlos Brown via Meck County Sheriff’s Office “It’s not a matter of something very subjective. They look at a lot of pieces of information and take someone through a battery of different psychological tests so that they’re also able to see that it’s a window of time where they have been in a certain mental state, not just in the moment. You cannot fake incompetency,” Johnson said.
Johnson says loved ones and supporters can feel like a suspect is getting away with a crime, but the main goal of incompetency is a pause.
“It is very possible that through treatment, which will be part of the next steps, that they can get to a place of competency, and then they would continue to go through trial,” she continued.
Johnson says those next steps include some type of court-ordered treatment, possibly in a secure psychiatric ward setting.
“And the goal is to help restore their competency or determine if they’re not in a place where they have the capacity to get back to that level of functioning,” she said.
The mental health expert says there are cases where someone may have been mentally incompetent at the moment, then they go through the court-ordered treatment, and competency is restored.
“Because they’re in the right setting. They have the right support. They might have the right medication. And that is the point that those charges could come back on the table, and then they are fit to stand trial.”
